title: As long as space remains: the vow to stay
hookLine: vows say 'till death us do part'; Shantideva's promise runs as long as space, and Matthew's Gospel has a neighbor to it
carry: the bodhisattva vow: stay while anyone suffers
tomorrow: a whole poem behind you. which one verse would you keep?

cards: A lease says twelve months. An old wedding service says "till death us do part." A friend at midnight says i'm always here for you, and mostly means it.

Every promise to stay comes with a length. Near the end of his poem, Shantideva names his. For as long as space remains, and for as long as living beings remain, may I remain too, to clear away the suffering of the world.

teach.h: AS LONG AS ANYONE NEEDS IT.
teach.b: So, the question: how long would you stay for someone? Shantideva's answer: as long as anyone needs it. Space doesn't run out, and in his verse, neither do the beings who need help.
This is the bodhisattva vow at full size. Not one lifetime of kindness, but staying, life after life, while anyone still suffers.
Notice it's said as a wish: may I remain. It's a direction to face, not a schedule to keep. And here a neighbor tradition says something that rhymes with it.

teach.h: MATTHEW: I AM WITH YOU ALWAY.
teach.b: At the very end of the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his followers: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." Two promises to stay as long as the world lasts.
That's what they share: a love that doesn't plan its exit. And here's the honest difference.

teach.h: A PROMISE GIVEN; A VOW TAKEN.
teach.b: In Matthew, Christians hear the risen Christ promising his presence; it's a promise given to them. Shantideva's is a vow taken: someone still on the path, wishing to remain and help across many lives.
One is received. One is made. Each means what it means in its own house, and neither has to become the other to be beautiful.

how: Tibetan Buddhists and others recite this verse, sometimes at the close of a teaching or with the bodhisattva vow; for Christians, Matthew 28:20 is the closing line of Matthew's Gospel.

games.q: what does “as long as space remains” mean?
o: a promise to stay with one partner for your whole life
a vow to keep helping for as long as beings exist
a teaching about how big the universe really is

games.q: two promises to stay — tap the pairs.
p: a love that doesn't plan its exit
a promise given; a vow taken

s: Shantideva's vow is for one lifetime of helping
it runs for as long as space and living beings remain.
Matthew's Gospel ends with Jesus promising to be with his followers always
"lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world."
the two promises mean exactly the same thing
they share a promise to stay. in Matthew, Christ promises his presence; Shantideva takes a vow.

games.q: a classmate hears both verses and says: "so Buddhism and Christianity teach the same thing." what's the fairest reply?
o: they share a promise to stay; one is Christ's promise, the other a vow.
yes, deep down every tradition teaches exactly the same thing.
no, they have nothing in common; one has God and one doesn't.
games.why: the honest answer holds both: a real likeness, a love that stays, and a real difference, a promise received and a vow made. no ranking needed.

practice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper. Write Shantideva's promise in your own words, as plainly as you'd text it, short enough to fit on the back of your hand. Then read it back once, slowly, and let it sit.

wordCard.voice: As long as space remains: Shantideva's vow to keep helping for as long as space and living beings last.

orig.note: Sanskrit: space, sky (Pali akasa, आकास). The verse measures the vow by it.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the bodhisattva vow, to stay while anyone suffers, a promise with no exit planned. Forty-nine of fifty.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.55 (for as long as space endures and living beings remain, may I too remain to dispel the misery of the world)
